title: The Model Is Not the Moat: Silicon Valley's Second AI Wave, Where the Money Starts Moving to Hardware
dek: Silicon Valley has reached a consensus: the model itself is neither a product nor a moat — what's valuable is the use case built on top of it. At the same time, the GPU shortage is pushing investment from software toward hardware, and big-company strategic investors are entering earlier than pure VCs.
why: Two people from the American tech world review Silicon Valley AI from both the technical and investment angles, with high information density — especially the second half on open-source strategy, regulatory posture and the differences between China and the US.
who: Chinese founders and investors watching AI startups and investment direction, and anyone who wants to understand models, applications, compute and the M&A landscape in Silicon Valley's second wave.
skip: From 47:25 to 48:46 they talk about Silicon Valley housing prices and Kevin moving house — low information density, skippable.

points.h: The model is not a product, and even less a moat
points.body: Kevin says a consensus has gradually formed in Silicon Valley: the model itself is not a product, you can't sell the model directly; and the model, big or small, is not actually a moat. The reason is that there are more and more open-source models — they may not be the best, but they're not much worse than the best, and open-source software usually iterates faster. So the companies that can really survive long term are the ones that treat the model as foundational software and build the use case on top of it into a product, rather than just making a feature. Xiaojun adds that the discussion in China has changed over the past few months too: a few months ago investors were still asking ‘the underlying layer is a general large model, so if I build a product on top of it, what's my moat’, and now the discussion has all become about products and applications.

points.h: The GPU shortage pushes investment from software to hardware
points.body: One shocking thing in the first half of the year was the GPU shortage on the hardware side, with NVIDIA alone holding the most core GPUs. Kevin observed that a lot of investment direction started shifting from software toward hardware, and many hardware-related startups are working on this. He judges that this shortage will be solved sooner or later, maybe in a year or two, but the hardware bottleneck affects both startups and big companies developing new products internally. The finer mechanism: for every GPU or set of GPUs you buy, you have to satisfy three audiences at once — the people doing research and building models, the users a beta product release has to satisfy, and the internal teams building applications — so internally reallocating GPU resource allocation is itself a big problem, never mind whether you can even buy them.

points.h: Copilot is a marketing position, not a replacement for people
points.body: Sophia says the Copilot concept isn't actually new — there was robotic process automation (RPA) before, but RPA never reached its expected potential, whereas Copilot is another level, and maybe RPA will finally work through Copilot. She points out that the Copilot concept is the autopilot on a plane — a person can take control and modify at any time, with AI helping alongside. Honestly, this is also a marketing positioning: because if AI is too strong, many industries in the US have already started worrying about whether it will replace their jobs, with the most attention on Hollywood writers and actors starting to march and strike, and journalists at some news organizations doing the same. So ‘I'm not trying to replace people, I'm just helping people do their work more efficiently’ is a very good position.

points.h: Two acquisitions: one offense, one defense
points.body: Several acquisitions in the first half of the year revealed different signals. Mosaic ML was bought by Databricks for about 1.2 billion, and Kevin's analogy is Facebook buying Instagram back then — also around a billion, with very few people: Mosaic maybe fifty or sixty people, while Instagram at the time was no more than twenty. The other is CaseText in the legal industry, bought by Thomson Reuters for 650 million in cash; Sophia says this company worked hard for ten years and ultimately, because of the generative AI wave, was acquired for cash. Kevin contrasts the two: Databricks is already a high-tech company, thinking about how to quickly open up the possibilities in AI — that's offense; Thomson Reuters is more about seeing its own industry changing — that's defense, thinking about how to make the business continue to survive.

points.h: Meituan bought Light Year Beyond, and no one in Silicon Valley discusses it
points.body: Xiaojun asks whether this acquisition is popular in Silicon Valley, and Kevin answers ‘what I saw was also in Chinese, but no one, no one really talks about it’ — he personally follows Chinese tech industry moves so he knows, but Silicon Valley itself already has enough M&A news, and not many people pay attention to China's moves. Xiaojun says Light Year Beyond was one of the large-model companies Chinese investors were most bullish on in the first half of the year, and the reason wasn't that the founder had a technical background, but that he was a very successful entrepreneur who co-founded Meituan, a company with a market cap in the hundreds of billions — in China it's very rare to have successfully started a company once and then enter large models so high-profile. Sophia thinks this Meituan acquisition has a slight emotional tint, since they're all old comrades from startups, and when you hit trouble you have to draw an endpoint and give an explanation, whereas the AI-related acquisitions and future IPOs seen in the US are relatively pure business logic, without much emotional tint.

points.h: Paper authors are lobbied out of academia by VCs to start companies
points.body: Kevin describes a very common pattern: behind every large model there's a paper, and people who like reading papers will look at exactly who wrote it; a month or two later, several of the people who wrote the paper get poached to do a startup, or some VC funds lobby them out and invest in them. The vast majority of these people still have fairly technical, research-leaning backgrounds. Kevin says his personal view is slightly pessimistic — he hopes they can quickly start pragmatically thinking about how to productize, how to bring the value of large models out through real real-life use cases, rather than just using VC money or big-company money to do a research project, otherwise it's still a bit of a shame.

points.h: The first-tier products are all priced by mature companies
points.body: Xiaojun asks what the first-tier products were in the first half of the year, and Sophia counts them off: Github Copilot set a price, competitor GitLab's similar copilot for assisting programmers also set a price, Salesforce's product set a price, Microsoft's Office Suite set a price, Adobe set a price, and Notion, this productivity tool, set a price, and AWS's own copilot called Code Whisper also counts as having set a price. Her criterion is: if you don't dare to price it, if it isn't sold separately, it doesn't count as a separate product. So this list is all mature companies, and not one completely new company has come out yet. She also says we are still at the infancy — it's still very, very early, and checking in again this time next year should give a different list.

points.h: Meta open-sources to erode other people's moats
points.body: Kevin discusses open source and closed source on two levels. Among the big players: companies building large models are still mostly closed source, just as the database industry started out mostly with closed-source solutions, like Oracle. Open source in competition is actually slowly lowering the moat of closed-source tech. The best example is why Meta works hard to open-source its own Llama — it isn't an enterprise services company itself, unlike Google and Microsoft which have their own cloud platforms and can directly package models into APIs and sell them; but it knows that if it only uses other people's models while its own model lags behind, that's bad for its future competitive positioning, so it open-sources all its models, which is actually about lowering the moat of the models of other competing big players, and at the same time it can iterate its own model quickly, because once open-sourced anyone can download it and build new models on top of it, and it can also absorb the iterative progress programmers bring.

points.h: This time Silicon Valley goes to Washington on its own; before it hid
points.body: Kevin observes one thing different about this AI wave from before: Silicon Valley companies, big or small, are much earlier in participating in regulation. Sam Altman has already done many hearings, Hugging Face's co-founder went to Congress for a hearing and also took part in the White House AI summit. He says that before, there always seemed to be some hostility — the farther from DC the better, best not to bother me, until you absolutely have to deal with them, rather than very proactively accepting Congress's invitation to hearings to express views. This may show that the whole of Silicon Valley is more mature, or that its relationship with DC is more productive, or it may be that everyone has many concerns about AI's future safety and regulatory issues and wants to talk to Congress first, to reduce the risk that the government actually puts out some fairly dumb policies that affect the whole industry's development.

Robotic process automation, technology that automates repetitive office processes, which had previously never met expectations.
